title: Federal Same-Sex Marriage Restriction and Annulment Program - LGBTQ+ Legal Recognition Elimination
description_short: Federal Same-Sex Marriage Restriction and Annulment Program - LGBTQ+ Legal Recognition Elimination
description_medium: Project 2025 promoted a family-policy vision centered on heterosexual, two-parent households, but its described proposals do not include an order annulling existing same-sex marriages or ending federal recognition. A federal annulment program and its legal mechanism therefore remain unverified, as do claims about lost marriage benefits.
description_long: Donald Trump implemented systematic restrictions on same-sex marriage recognition while establishing federal annulment programs that enabled states to void existing marriages through Project 2025's plan to prioritize 'heterosexual, two-parent families' as exclusively legitimate while eliminating federal protections and benefits for LGBTQ+ couples and their children. The comprehensive marriage restriction represented Trump's implementation of conservative family ideology that classified same-sex relationships as inferior while enabling faith-based discrimination through federal grant programs that excluded LGBTQ+ families from adoption services, family support programs, and marriage-related benefits. The same-sex marriage targeting included eliminating federal recognition of marriage equality while allowing states to implement 'religious freedom' laws that enabled government officials to refuse marriage licenses, adoption services, and family benefits to LGBTQ+ couples based on conservative religious objections. Trump's marriage discrimination violated constitutional equal protection principles by treating same-sex couples as second-class citizens while eliminating legal protections for LGBTQ+ families including hospital visitation rights, inheritance protections, and parental recognition that had provided security and stability for children in same-sex parent households. The LGBTQ+ family targeting created what civil rights advocates called systematic elimination of marriage equality through federal policies that enabled state discrimination while prioritizing conservative religious ideology over constitutional equal protection and family welfare. The marriage restriction represented Project 2025's vision of family policy controlled by conservative religious definition rather than constitutional equality, transforming marriage from legal contract with equal protection into religious institution that excluded LGBTQ+ Americans while eliminating federal recognition and benefits that had historically provided legal security for diverse American families.
subcategory: LGBTQ+ Marriage Rights Elimination and Family Discrimination
notes: Needs context: the linked material does not document a federal marriage-annulment policy or its legal mechanism.

title: Donald Trump flies on Epstein's private jet with accused pedophile
description_short: Donald Trump flies on Epstein's private jet with accused pedophile
description_medium: Flight logs unsealed in August 2019 show Donald Trump, Jeffrey Epstein, Glenn and Eva Dubin, Ghislaine Maxwell and other passengers traveling from Palm Beach to New Jersey on Epstein’s private jet on January 5, 1997. The entries list the plane, route and passengers. Their release came among court records unsealed in a defamation case; a flight log does not describe what passengers did or discussed.
description_long: A handwritten flight-log entry dated January 5, 1997, records a trip from Palm Beach International Airport to Newark Liberty International Airport on a Gulfstream II owned by Jeffrey Epstein. The listed passengers included Donald Trump, Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell, Mark Epstein, Glenn Dubin, Eva Dubin and a person whose name was transcribed as “Didler” or “Didier.” The log became public in August 2019 when nearly 2,000 documents from a defamation lawsuit were unsealed. It records the date, route, aircraft and passengers entered by the person keeping it, but gives no account of their conversations or the purpose of the trip. The flight log establishes that these passengers shared a flight; it offers no account of their conduct beyond the recorded travel. Flight records have been examined alongside other evidence about Epstein’s contacts and movements. This particular entry contributes a dated route and passenger list to that record, while questions about the passengers’ knowledge or actions require evidence beyond the flight itself.

title: Trump: GOP Senators, Conway, and campaign manager test positive for COVID-19
description_short: Trump: GOP Senators, Conway, and campaign manager test positive for COVID-19
description_medium: On October 3, 2020, campaign manager Bill Stepien, former adviser Kellyanne Conway and Senators Thom Tillis and Mike Lee announced positive COVID-19 tests. They had attended the September 26 White House Rose Garden event for Amy Coney Barrett’s Supreme Court nomination, along with other people who later tested positive, including President Trump and the first lady. The timing prompted concern about an event-related cluster, though the exposure location for each person remained unknown.
description_long: Several senior figures connected to the Trump administration and campaign reported positive COVID-19 tests on October 3, 2020. They included campaign manager Bill Stepien, former White House adviser Kellyanne Conway, Republican Senators Thom Tillis and Mike Lee, and University of Notre Dame president John Jenkins. Conway, Tillis and Lee had attended the September 26 Rose Garden event announcing Amy Coney Barrett’s Supreme Court nomination. President Donald Trump, First Lady Melania Trump, adviser Hope Hicks and Republican National Committee chair Ronna McDaniel had also tested positive in the days before. The number of cases among people connected to the event prompted questions about precautions at the White House and the administration’s response to the outbreak. The overlap in timing raised concern about a possible cluster, but the exposure location for each individual remained unknown. The illnesses also focused attention on the risks of large gatherings during the pandemic, particularly as officials who communicated safety guidance and their political associates became ill.

title: Trump admin reverses guidance on protecting LGBTQ students from school meal discrimination
description_short: Trump admin reverses guidance on protecting LGBTQ students from school meal discrimination
description_medium: On July 7, 2025, the USDA Food and Nutrition Service rescinded a 2022 interpretation that treated discrimination based on sex as covering sexual orientation and gender identity in child-nutrition programs. The guidance had applied to school meal programs, including the National School Lunch Program. USDA said the prior interpretation was unlawful; advocates disputed that view, citing the Supreme Court’s Bostock reasoning and lower-court applications to Title IX. The reversal raised concerns about protection for LGBTQ students receiving meals.
description_long: The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food and Nutrition Service announced on July 7, 2025, that it was rescinding a 2022 interpretation of sex discrimination in child-nutrition programs. The earlier guidance included discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and applied to programs such as the National School Lunch Program, which serves tens of millions of students. USDA’s memo said the Biden-era interpretation was unlawful. Civil-rights advocates disputed that conclusion, pointing to the Supreme Court’s 2020 decision in Bostock v. Clayton County, which held that Title VII’s prohibition on sex discrimination covers sexual orientation and gender identity, and to lower courts that applied similar reasoning under Title IX. A 2024 Supreme Court injunction had affected the 2022 policy, while lower courts continued to recognize LGBTQ protections under Title IX. The rescission changed USDA guidance for school meal providers but did not settle the broader legal question of how federal sex-discrimination law applies. Advocates warned that LGBTQ students could face discrimination in access to meals. Schools and nutrition programs now face questions about which protections remain and how complaints should be handled.
